metadata.title: Train the Teacher
metadata.subtitle: An argument published, then audited — and the sentences that did not survive
metadata.purpose: Films Nik Bear Brown's May 2026 skepticism.ai essay 'Not the App. Not the Ban. Train the Teacher.' together with the September 2026 adversarial evidence audit commissioned against it. The film's subject is the pair: what the audit corrected, what survived, and the study nobody has run.
metadata.vox_rationale: VOX LAW: the evidence in this film is statutes, cost reports and effect sizes. A pantry still could only be texture here, so there are none and there is no SHOPPING.md. Every beat renders.
sources: Nik Bear Brown, 'Not the App. Not the Ban. Train the Teacher.', skepticism.ai, 2026-05-16
metadata.source_precedence: Where the essay and the audit disagree, the AUDIT governs.

beats.act: COLD OPEN
beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Bear. In May, Bear published an argument about phones, school technology, and where the money should actually go. Then he did something most people who publish an argument never do. He had it attacked. Not reviewed. Attacked — under instructions to fix or kill every number in it. This film is what came back.
beats.new_visual_element: ClaudeComposerAsk — the ask, answered

props.command: Here is an argument I published. Run an adversarial evidence audit on it. Do not support it — try to break it.
output: Four of its sentences do not.
And one whole act of the case is missing.

show.event: Three output lines land in sequence

beats.act: THE OVERVIEW
beats.narration_text: Here is the whole film in one breath. The essay says the binding constraint on technology in schools is teacher capability — not the device policy, not the platform. The audit says that recommendation is defensible. It also says four of the sentences carrying it are wrong, and the study that would actually prove it has not been run by anyone.
beats.new_visual_element: BrutalistHesitantWriter — the overview, corrected on screen

props.text:
This is a film about an essay that was right.
It is about how much of the evidence
for being right was actually there.
props.replacementWords: an argument that survived its own audit

show.event: 'an essay that was right' types out
The clause turns terracotta and deletes
'an argument that survived its own audit' types in

beats.act: ACT I — TWO ANSWERS, ONE QUESTION
beats.narration_text: Start with the argument as published, because the audit only means something if you take the argument seriously first.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqSegmentCard — Act I

beats.act: ACT I — TWO ANSWERS, ONE QUESTION
beats.narration_text: The policy debate offered two answers to one question. Technology is harming students — what do we do? Answer one: ban the phone. Answer two: buy a better platform. Both answers arrive with force. Neither of them reaches the classroom, because neither of them is about the person standing in it.
beats.new_visual_element: TtTwoAnswers — both answers drive in and stop short

props.question: Technology is harming students. What do we do?

left.name: Ban the phone.
left.sub: Remove the device. Restore the room.

right.name: Buy the platform.
right.sub: Adaptive software. The right tutor. Trust the algorithm.

props.gapLabel: neither answer is about the teacher
props.note: The essay's opening move: both answers address the equipment.
props.spark: One question. Two misses.

show.event: Both arrest short of centre — the gap holds
Terracotta bracket closes on the empty middle

beats.act: ACT I — TWO ANSWERS, ONE QUESTION
beats.narration_text: The best causal evidence on bans comes from one large Florida district. And it found something uncomfortable. The disciplinary cost lands in year one. The academic benefit shows up in year two. For a student suspended out of a critical semester, later is not the same as yes.
beats.new_visual_element: TtFrontLoaded — the cost track rises a year before the benefit track

props.title: The cost and the benefit are not on the same clock.
props.bandLabel: paid here — collected a year later
props.note: Figlio & Özek — one Florida district. The timing is the finding.
props.spark: Front-loaded.

show.event: Cost line climbs across year one, then holds
Benefit line sits flat — visibly doing nothing
Benefit line rises in year two
Terracotta band fills the interval where cost exists alone

beats.act: ACT I — TWO ANSWERS, ONE QUESTION
beats.narration_text: Then the essay finds a blank. Phone-ban statutes carve out an exemption for educational purposes. The teacher is handed the judgement — in the moment, at nine in the morning, with a room watching. The essay's charge is that the laws hand over the decision without handing over the definition.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqDefinitionDrop — the exemption with its centre missing

props.title: What the exemption says
parts: an exemption exists for educational purposes
the teacher decides, live, case by case
props.note: The essay's sharpest move. Act II narrows it.
props.spark: A decision without a definition.

show.event: The three given parts land in sequence
The gap is left visibly open
The missing term drops into it in terracotta

beats.act: ACT I — TWO ANSWERS, ONE QUESTION
beats.narration_text: So the essay asks for three things. Supervised technology time that replaces what the ban removed. A definition written before the rule is enforced. And sustained, subject-specific training for teachers in how AI changes what teaching requires. That is the claim. Now watch it get taken apart.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqLevers — the three asks, standing before the audit

props.title: The essay's three asks

levers.name: Access
levers.sub: supervised, teacher-led technology time — scaled to what the ban removed

levers.name: Definition
levers.sub: write what 'educational' means before enforcing what it excludes

levers.name: Training
levers.sub: sustained, subject-specific professional learning in AI

props.note: Three asks. The audit rules on each of them separately.
props.spark: The argument, standing.

show.event: Three columns rise on a stagger, terracotta top rules
Each subtitle types beneath its column

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: The audit did not argue with the conclusion. It went after the sentences.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqSegmentCard — Act II

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: First it refused to rule on the argument as a whole. It cut the claim into seven pieces and ruled on each one separately — because an argument that is sixty percent right is not sixty percent true. It has a specific list of parts that hold and a specific list that do not.
beats.new_visual_element: TtVerdictGrid — the claim decomposed, each row stamped

props.title: The claim, decomposed

rows.claim: Ban costs are front-loaded and unevenly distributed
Teacher support makes or breaks EdTech
Districts overspend on hardware versus training
Most teachers lack the skills to use AI
Sustained AI training is affordable inside current budgets
AI-specific teacher training improves student learning

props.note: Seven pieces, seven verdicts. The last one is the one that matters.
props.spark: Rule on the parts, not the mood.

show.event: Rows land top to bottom on a stagger
Each verdict stamps in behind its row

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: Start with the number the essay opened on. Suspensions up thirty percent for Black boys. The authors' own account says something narrower. In-school suspensions, for Black students. And for out-of-school suspensions — the ones that remove a child from the building — no significant effect at all.
beats.new_visual_element: TtCorrection — the opening statistic, struck and restated

props.before: In the first year of the ban, suspensions increased 30 percent for
props.corrected: About 30 percent — for IN-SCHOOL suspensions, among Black students. No significant effect on out-of-school suspensions.
props.citation: Figlio & Özek, authors' own May 2026 account
props.note: Narrower subgroup. Narrower outcome. The disparity is still real.
props.spark: The sharpest number in the piece.

show.event: The published sentence holds on the page
The correction card drops in beneath

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: The scope shrank too. This is one large Florida district, comparing schools that used phones more against schools that used them less. Not a statewide evaluation. The overall academic difference is about one percentile point — and it was not significant for girls, or for elementary students. So all groups benefited is not what the study says.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqLedger — the study's real scope, line by line

props.title: What the study actually covers

rows.label: Schools with more pre-ban phone use vs. less

props.note: Still worth doing. Just not what the sentence claimed.
props.spark: Read the scope, not the headline.

show.event: The two terracotta rows resolve last

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: Next, the study the essay used as its clincher. Free software, forty-six dollars a student, all of it teacher training, and it moved state maths scores. The audit read the cost report. The forty-six dollars covers platform maintenance and implementation support as well. The intervention was a package, and you cannot pull the training out of it.
beats.new_visual_element: TtCorrection — the clincher, restated as a package

props.before: The only implementation cost was $46 per student —
props.after: . The platform didn't do it. The training did.
props.corrected: $46.23 per student, 2021 dollars — including platform maintenance and implementation support. 63 schools; a 0.10 SD later gain in 8th-grade maths.
props.citation: Feng, Weiser & Collins, WestEd cost analysis, 2024
props.note: A price of zero does not make the software causally irrelevant.
props.spark: The clincher, re-read.

show.event: Strike sweeps 'entirely in teacher professional development'

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: Then the equity statistic. More than half of students without home Wi-Fi get online by phone. Pull the camera back and look at the denominator. Out of a hundred children, four are smartphone-only and three have nothing. The fraction is real. But it is a fraction of seven, not a fraction of the student body.
beats.new_visual_element: TtDenominator — the headline pulls back to reveal its denominator

props.headlineClaim: "more than half of students without home Wi-Fi"
props.correction: 57% of the seven — not of the classroom
props.note: NCES, 2021 ACS estimates, ages 3–18. The date is a caveat.
props.spark: Always ask what the percent is of.

show.event: The camera pulls back; the headline shrinks
The seven flagged squares land first
The other ninety-three fill in behind them

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: The essay's best line was that every one of those laws leaves the exemption undefined and not one state fills it in. Texas has no general classroom educational-use exception at all — it names disability plans, documented medical need, and safety. New York does let a school authorise a specific educational purpose. The blank is real in places. It is not universal.
beats.new_visual_element: TtCorrection — the universal claim, narrowed to a real one

props.before: Every one of those state laws contains an exemption for educational purposes.
props.corrected: Texas names specific exceptions and no general educational-use carve-out. New York permits authorisation for a specific educational purpose.
props.citation: Texas Education Agency, HB 1481 guidance · New York Education Law §2803
props.note: The teacher-judgement problem survives. 'Not one' does not.
props.spark: A universal claim needs a universal check.

show.event: The two statutes drop in beneath

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: And the essay said no new law addressed the enforcement problem that killed New York's first ban a decade ago. New York's own statute does. It bars suspending a student purely for using a device, and it requires the district to report enforcement by demographic group and file a plan if the disparities are significant.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqRingWord — the claim, and the clause that contradicts it

props.before: "None of the new laws addressed what broke the policy
props.attribution: the essay — contradicted by New York Education Law §2803(7)
props.note: Paper safeguards are not proof. They are not nothing either.
props.spark: Check the statute, not the memory.

show.event: Terracotta ring draws around 'the first time'

beats.act: ACT II — THEN SOMEBODY AUDITED IT
beats.narration_text: One more. The thirty-seventy rule — thirty percent on hardware, seventy on people. It is a real recommendation from a real brief. From two thousand and two. Twenty-four years before the sentence that cites it, and about human infrastructure generally, not about an AI budget.
beats.new_visual_element: TtCorrection — a live recommendation revealed as a historical one

props.before: WestEd recommends 30 percent on hardware and 70 percent on people —
props.wrong: a current benchmark most districts invert
props.corrected: Investing in Technology: The Learning Return — WestEd policy brief, August 2002, citing Wahl (2000). Historical guidance about human infrastructure, not a modern AI budget optimum.
props.verdict: KEEP THE PRINCIPLE — DATE THE SOURCE
props.citation: and it cannot describe how districts spend today
props.note: The principle may hold. It has not been retested since.
props.spark: An undated citation is a warning sign.

show.event: The 2002 brief drops in with its real title

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: Five corrections in, the obvious question. Is there anything left?
beats.new_visual_element: ReqSegmentCard — Act III

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: Yes. The core of it. Sixty studies with causal designs, pooled: coaching moves what teachers do by about half a standard deviation, and moves what students learn by about a fifth. That is a real effect from a real synthesis, and it is the strongest brick in the essay's wall.
beats.new_visual_element: TtEffectBars — the coaching meta-analysis, both outcomes

props.title: Teacher coaching — pooled causal effects
props.scaleNote: STANDARD DEVIATIONS · BARS SCALED TO THE LARGER EFFECT
props.note: Kraft, Blazar & Hogan (2018) — 60 studies, causal designs only.
props.spark: The brick that holds.

show.event: Achievement bar grows to 0.18 in terracotta

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: But read the same paper for its warning. The effect is not a constant. Much of the evidence sits in early literacy and small trials — and as the programmes get bigger, the effect gets smaller. Whatever coaching does, it does less of it at the scale a district would actually have to buy.
beats.new_visual_element: TtScaleDecay — the effect shrinking as the programme grows

props.title: The effect is not a constant.

stops.caption: tight conditions, close supervision, often early literacy
the version a district could actually run

props.note: Direction, not a number — no pooled effect per scale tier exists.
props.spark: Scale decay.

show.event: The bar rises to its small-trial height
The bar shrinks in place, ghost outline left behind
Reading settles at the lower value

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: And here is the study that should stop anyone from saying more training, and stopping there. Around two hundred fourth-grade teachers. Ninety-three hours of maths professional development — content, collaboration, individual feedback. Teacher knowledge went up. Some practices improved. Student achievement did not move.
beats.new_visual_element: TtNullResult — one meter climbs, the other does not

props.title: 93 hours. Two outcomes.

left.label: Teacher knowledge
left.caption: improved, along with some observed practices

props.note: IES elementary maths PD evaluation. Design principles, not guarantees.
props.spark: The word 'sustained' is not a mechanism.

show.event: Right meter is given the same window and does not move
Terracotta flat line draws across the right baseline

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: So the honest version of the ASSISTments result is not the training did it. It is that a package — software, training, a warm-up year, and ongoing support — moved eighth-grade maths by a tenth of a standard deviation for about forty-six dollars a student. That is still a good buy. It is just not an argument for training alone.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqLedger — the intervention listed as what it actually was

props.title: What was actually bought
props.note: Four ingredients, one result. The design cannot separate them.
props.spark: Supported implementation.

show.event: Components land one at a time
The result row lands in terracotta

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: There is one more piece of good news, and it is newer. Give tutors live AI assistance during a session and mastery of the lesson topic rises four points — nine points for the students of the lowest-rated tutors. The help lands where the expertise is thinnest. End-of-year maths, though, showed no significant difference.
beats.new_visual_element: TtEffectBars — real-time assistance, both readings and the null

props.title: Live AI assistance to tutors
props.note: Wang et al., Tutor CoPilot (working paper) — 900 tutors, 1,800 students.
props.spark: Help arrives where skill is thin.

show.event: The null end-of-year result lands in the note

beats.act: ACT III — WHAT SURVIVED
beats.narration_text: Notice what every surviving result has in common. None of them is a study of training. They are studies of supported implementation — the tool and the human capacity to use it, bought together, evaluated together. That is a real finding. It is a different finding from the one the essay claimed.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqRingWord — the phrase the evidence actually supports

props.before: What the evidence supports is not training. It is
props.after: — the tool and the capacity, bought together.
props.note: Complementary investments, not a spending formula.
props.spark: Change the noun, keep the policy.

show.event: Terracotta ring draws around the phrase

beats.act: ACT IV — THE HOLE IN THE MIDDLE
beats.narration_text: Which leaves the sentence the whole essay is built on. And that one has a different problem.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqSegmentCard — Act IV

beats.act: ACT IV — THE HOLE IN THE MIDDLE
beats.narration_text: The claim is that training teachers in AI improves what students learn. Go looking for the experiment that shows it. Trials of coaching — yes. Trials of maths training — yes. Trials of AI tools with tutors — yes. Trials of AI-specific teacher training measured on student outcomes. Almost none.
beats.new_visual_element: TtAbsence — the query, and the results dissolving

props.query: trials: AI-specific teacher professional development → student outcomes
ghosts: AI tutoring trials — not teacher training
AI assistance for tutors — not durable skill
props.note: Not that training fails. That nobody ran the study.
props.spark: Look for the study. Notice it is not there.

show.event: The query types into the field
Candidate rows rise one at a time
Each dissolves as its disqualifier lands

beats.act: ACT IV — THE HOLE IN THE MIDDLE
beats.narration_text: Which changes what kind of sentence this is. The essay wrote: this is not a philosophical claim, it is what the evidence shows. The audit's answer is that it is a defensible bet. Those are both respectable things to publish. They are not the same thing, and the reader deserves to know which one they are being handed.
beats.new_visual_element: TtCorrection — a finding, restated as a bet

props.before: This is not a philosophical claim.
props.wrong: It is what the evidence shows
props.corrected: It is a defensible bet, extrapolated from adjacent evidence — coaching, supported implementation, and teacher self-report. The direct study does not exist yet.
props.citation: and a bet is still worth making; it is just labelled differently
props.note: The recommendation survives this. The epistemics of the sentence do not.
props.spark: Say which one you are selling.

show.event: Strike sweeps 'It is what the evidence shows'

beats.act: ACT IV — THE HOLE IN THE MIDDLE
beats.narration_text: The essay's closing analogy has the same shape. Doctors have mandatory continuing education, so teachers should too — and teaching has no such system. Illinois requires a hundred and twenty hours for licence renewal. The infrastructure exists. The argument that it should be better is a different argument from the one the essay made.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqRingWord — the analogy's missing premise

props.attribution: the essay — Illinois requires 120 hours for licence renewal
props.note: Massachusetts counts 50 credits per two-year cycle, not 50 a year.
props.spark: The system exists. Argue about its quality.

show.event: Terracotta ring draws around the false premise

beats.act: ACT IV — THE HOLE IN THE MIDDLE
beats.narration_text: Even the survey the essay leans on says more than it was asked to. Seventy percent of teachers not using AI say they lack the knowledge and skills. Ask the same teachers a different question — what stops you doing professional learning at all — and two-thirds say other responsibilities, three in five say scheduling. The knowledge gap is real. So is the calendar.
beats.new_visual_element: TtEffectBars — the three barriers, and the two questions behind them

props.title: Two questions, two answers

data.label: Not using AI: lack the knowledge

props.caveat: Row one answers a different survey question from rows two and three.
props.note: OECD TALIS 2024, US. Row one is a different survey item.
props.spark: Buy the hours as well as the content.

beats.act: ACT V — WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT
beats.narration_text: An audit that only subtracts is half an audit. Here is the study that would settle it.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqSegmentCard — Act V

beats.act: ACT V — WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT
beats.narration_text: Give every school the same tools and the same basic orientation. Then randomise which schools also get coaching and protected time to collaborate. That comparison isolates the thing actually in dispute — not whether technology helps, but whether the support wrapped around it is what earns the gain.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqLevers — the design that isolates the disputed ingredient

props.title: The study nobody has run

levers.name: Hold constant
levers.sub: same tools, same essential orientation, every school

levers.name: Randomise
levers.sub: coaching and protected collaborative time, by school

levers.name: Measure
levers.sub: student learning on curriculum-aligned tests taken without AI

blocked: whether the tool alone works — that needs a separate arm
props.blockedLabel: what this design still cannot tell you
props.note: Pre-register the outcomes. Power it for achievement, not for teacher confidence.
props.spark: Isolate the disputed ingredient.

show.event: Three columns rise on a stagger
The blocked row lands in grey — the honest limit

beats.act: ACT V — WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT
beats.narration_text: And measure six things, not one. Did teachers improve. Did students learn. Did the learning last. Did the teacher's judgement last once the AI was taken away. Was access equal. And could the school actually afford to keep doing it.
beats.new_visual_element: ReqLedger — the six questions the evaluation has to answer

props.title: Six questions, six measures
props.note: Confidence, time saved and usage are secondary outcomes. Never the headline.
props.spark: Assisted performance is not learning.

show.event: The durability row resolves in terracotta

beats.act: ACT V — WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT
beats.narration_text: And name what would prove the thesis wrong, because a claim that cannot lose is not a claim. Run that trial. If the coached schools and the uncoached schools land on the same student results, then the money belongs in the tools after all, and the essay was wrong.
beats.new_visual_element: TtNullResult — the falsifying result, drawn in advance

props.title: What would prove it wrong
props.inputLabel: same tools · same orientation · coaching randomised by school
props.note: Nobody is running it. The audit's most useful sentence.
props.spark: A claim that cannot lose is not a claim.

show.event: Terracotta line names the falsifying outcome

beats.act: VERDICT
beats.narration_text: So the verdict. The recommendation survives — invest in the capacity to use the tools, not just the tools. What did not survive is the evidence base as it was described: a subgroup narrowed, a cost attributed to the wrong ingredient, a universal claim that two statutes disprove, a benchmark from two thousand and two, and a finding that turns out to be a bet. The essay is better after the audit than before it. That is what an audit is for.
beats.new_visual_element: ClaudeVerdictArtifact — the verdict page

artifactLines: The recommendation holds: buy capacity alongside tools, not instead of them.
The Florida figure is in-school suspensions, Black students, one district.
The $46.23 bought a package — software, PD, warm-up year, support.
'Not one state defines it' is disproved by Texas and New York.
The 30/70 rule is a 2002 recommendation, not a current measurement.
'What the evidence shows' is really a defensible bet — no direct trial exists.
FALSIFIABLE: randomise coaching on top of identical tools. Equal results kill it.

show.event: Artifact window opens on the cream stage

beats.act: YOUR TURN
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take something you have published — a post, a memo, a proposal — and do not ask Claude whether it is good. Ask it to run an adversarial audit: decompose the argument into separate claims, rule on each one, and find every number that does not mean what the sentence says it means. Ask it to tell you which of your claims is a finding and which is a bet. That is the whole method in this film, and it works on anything you wrote.
beats.new_visual_element: ClaudeComposerAsk — the viewer's prompt, read aloud

props.command: Here is something I published. Run an adversarial evidence audit: decompose it into separate claims, rule on each, verify every number against its actual source, and tell me which claims are findings and which are bets.
